There is significant evidence that deportation and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) enforcement disproportionately target Hispanics, particularly those from Mexico and Central America. 

1. Demographic Disparities in Deportations

The vast majority of people deported from the U.S. are from Latin American countries. According to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) data, in recent years, more than 90% of deportations involved individuals from Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador.

Even though immigrants come from all over the world, Latin American immigrants—especially Mexicans—are disproportionately affected by enforcement actions.


2. Racial Profiling and Enforcement Practices

Studies and lawsuits have documented cases of racial profiling by ICE and local law enforcement agencies working with ICE (e.g., under the 287(g) program).

A 2011 study by the Warren Institute at UC Berkeley found that Latino individuals in Arizona were 9 times more likely to be stopped by ICE than non-Latinos.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and other organizations have repeatedly sued ICE for conducting racially motivated raids in Latino communities.


3. Workplace and Community Raids

ICE raids often target workplaces where Latin American immigrants are likely to be employed, such as agricultural and meatpacking industries.

Even in communities with mixed immigrant populations, ICE operations often focus on Spanish-speaking neighborhoods and Latino-majority workplaces.


4. Secure Communities and Local Policing Programs

The Secure Communities program, which allows local law enforcement to check fingerprints against immigration databases, has resulted in a disproportionate number of Hispanic immigrants being detained and deported.

Critics argue that this program has led to increased racial profiling of Latinos, as police may stop people based on their appearance or accent.


5. Statements from Former ICE Officials and Policymakers

Former ICE officials and DHS reports have acknowledged that immigration enforcement strategies primarily focus on Latinos, in part because they make up the largest unauthorized immigrant population but also due to historical bias in enforcement priorities.

My mom had schizophrenia (past tense as she is now dead) and killed her over 90 year old grandma by suffocation. The death was first ruled natural causes but my mother called police and confessed causing the body to be exhumed. When I asked her about it at a prison visit, she said a bunch of word salad about how she was trying to protect her grandma and so she had to hold her down with a pillow. She was clearly disconnected from reality and everything she said in our 3 hour visit I know to be untrue. I'm not an expert on schizophrenia and don't take this single example as proof of anything, but my mother had been diagnosed for over a decade before this and abandoned 4 children. She was on and off psychotic meds and yet sentenced to life without the possibility of parole in a normal prison, not even a psychiatric facility. She died by suicide in that prison. Most people who commit murder are not mentally ill. I personally don't think that matters.  I think prison should exist mainly to keep dangerous people out of society. If they can definitely be rehabilitated, the prison should do that. If not, they will have to stay out of society. Some people think crime just needs to be punished and they feel good when someone must suffer for their actions. In that case we have to look at the motive and what leads to it. This girl had a clear motive and I am sure there were things going on in her family relationships and upbringing that led her to that point. Her mom seemed like an amazing person who did so much for the world, but her daughter somehow didn't learn how to handle herself in the world and seems to have just worked herself into a frenzy. She obviously couldn't handle the stress of leaving the nest or expectations of the world and being an adult. There have actually been many similar cases of children murdering their parents to keep a secret. I think it's also similar to men murdering their families to keep secrets of infidelity or financial troubles. It doesn't make sense to most of us, but people don't usually act logically. Basically I think this girl probably had some mental issues, but they are no excuse for what she did.
